newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook- coming up for air after plunge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook- coming up for air after plunge.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices are expected to come up for air this week after recent sharp losses, with relatively expensive foreign crude, steady gasoline demand and short-covering ahead of the OPEC ministers' meeting later this month providing some temporary relief, traders and analysts said on Monday.

"The market's still under pressure until proven otherwise, but I don't see a whole lot more downside here. It's getting oversold," said Tom Bentz, head of energy trading at High Yield Analytics in New York.

The recovery which pushed West Texas Intermediate back above $22 a barrel in May well and truly petered out at the start of last week. Front-month WTI pluned $2.20, or more than 10 percent, to a 15-month low and was down slightly again on Monday, with July trading around $18.60-70.

The cash price for WTI/Cushing was running 18-22 cents ahead of the July future quote, reflecting the now-chronic premium for exchange-for-physical (EFP) transactions. August EFPs were fetching around 10-14 cents premium.
The premiums reflect ongoing jitters about some two million barrels of foreign crude that were delivered against the May and June NYMEX contracts but were never absorbed by refiners.
"Until someone takes the foreign crude and finds an economical way to run it, you'll see these EFPs at strong levels," a Houston broker said.

The July contract expiry on June 20 is likely to witness more redeliveries, traders said. In the meantime, most U.S. storage tanks are already full with foreign and domestic barrels, leaving even more crude hovering in the market looking for a home.

A closed arbitrage from the North Sea has lifted some of the pressure off domestic fundamentals, however, giving U.S. refiners fewer choices if not fewer barrels to satisfy record-high crude runs, traders said.

Brent was assessed around 70 cents a barrel under WTI/Cushing on a delivered basis for July, prompting most refiners to opt for less-pricey domestic grades like Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James or regional crudes like Colombia's Cusiana.

Gasoline demand is another factor that's likely to keep prices above water for now, traders said. This seasonal thirst for gasoline, however, is being tempered by record refinery capacity utilization of 104 percent, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.

Despite recent technical strides, analysts are still wary about unplanned outages. "The higher the capacity utilization, the higher the probability that any outage will have an impact on price," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York.
Finally, this week's outlook will be colored by a regular meeting of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) set for late June 25.
"I think nothing will happen there other than talking the market up," said Brown. "But there's usually some stability and short-covering before the meetings."

OPEC's persistent violation of its own production ceiling, coupled with the United Nations' recent renewal of the Iraqi oil-for-food deal, should reinforce the market's bearish tone in the weeks and months ahead, analysts said.
"The lower the price goes, the more Iraqi oil has to be sold," said Brown. As in the first round, Iraq has a limit of $2 billion on proceeds from humanitarian oil sales over a six-month period.
